prompts.title: Positioning statement and messaging pillars
prompts.description: Turn what you know about your product, customer and competitors into a sharp positioning statement plus three provable messaging pillars.
prompts.body:
You are a product marketer helping me define positioning for {{product}}.

Context
- Target customer: {{customer}}
- The problem they have today: {{problem}}
- What we do differently: {{differentiator}}
- Alternatives they use now (including doing nothing): {{alternatives}}
- Proof we can point to (numbers, customers, features, awards): {{proof}}

Task
1. Write three candidate positioning statements using this frame: "For [target customer] who [need], [product] is a [category] that [key benefit]. Unlike [alternative], we [primary differentiator]."
2. Recommend one and explain in two sentences why it is the most defensible.
3. Give three messaging pillars for the recommended statement. For each pillar include: a short headline, the customer-facing claim, and the specific proof that supports it. If the proof I gave does not support a claim, say so and name the evidence I would need.
4. List two claims I should avoid because they are generic or unprovable.

Rules
- Use plain, concrete language. No "revolutionary", "seamless", "cutting-edge" or "all-in-one" unless I used them.
- Do not invent statistics, customers or features. Mark any assumption as an assumption.
- Tone for the final copy: {{tone}}.

Output format: a heading per step, statements as a numbered list, pillars as a table with columns Headline, Claim, Proof.
Only ask me a question first if a missing input would make the statement misleading.

variables.label: Product or company
variables.default: Plotline, a project planning app for small design studios

variables.label: Target customer
variables.default: Studio owners and project leads at 5-30 person design agencies

variables.label: Their core problem
variables.default: They plan projects in spreadsheets and chat, so deadlines slip and nobody sees workload clashes until it is too late.

variables.label: What we do differently
variables.default: Plotline builds the schedule from the actual team calendar and flags overbooked weeks automatically.

variables.label: Alternatives they use
variables.default: Spreadsheets, Trello boards, Asana, and gut feel

variables.label: Proof points
variables.default: Setup takes about 20 minutes; 140 studios use it; customers report 2 fewer missed deadlines per quarter in our survey of 38 users
variables.help: Only include what you can back up.

variables.label: Tone
variables.default: Confident and plain-spoken

prompts.exampleOutput:
## 1. Candidate statements
1. For design studio leads who juggle many projects at once, Plotline is a planning app that shows overbooked weeks before they become missed deadlines. Unlike spreadsheets and Trello boards, we build the schedule from your real team calendar.
2. For small agency owners tired of chasing status in chat, Plotline is a project planner that keeps deadlines and workload in one view. Unlike Asana, it takes about 20 minutes to set up and needs no process overhaul.
3. For project leads at 5-30 person studios, Plotline is a scheduling tool that turns the team calendar into a live capacity map. Unlike gut feel, it warns you when a promise cannot be kept.

## 2. Recommendation
Statement 1. It names the concrete pain (overbooked weeks) and the one mechanism competitors lack (calendar-driven scheduling), and both are demonstrable in a demo.

## 3. Messaging pillars
| Headline | Claim | Proof |
|---|---|---|
| See clashes early | Overbooked weeks are flagged automatically | Calendar-driven scheduling (product behavior) |
| Set up in an afternoon | Go from zero to a live plan in about 20 minutes | Setup time; 140 studios in use |
| Fewer missed deadlines | Studios report fewer slips | 2 fewer per quarter, survey of 38 users (note sample size when quoting) |

## 4. Claims to avoid
- "The only planner built for creatives": unprovable.
- "Eliminates missed deadlines": your own data shows a reduction, not elimination.
prompts.notes: Forcing each pillar to name its proof exposes weak claims before they reach a landing page. Re-run with a different tone or a single competitor to see how the angle shifts.

prompts.title: Landing page copy critique
prompts.description: Paste your landing page copy and get a blunt, prioritized critique of clarity, proof and calls to action, with rewritten examples.
prompts.body:
Act as a conversion copywriter reviewing a landing page. Be direct and specific. I want fixes, not praise.

Page goal: {{goal}}
Visitor profile and where they come from: {{visitor}}
Offer: {{offer}}

Page copy, top to bottom:
"""
{{page_copy}}
"""

Review it in this order:
1. First-five-seconds test: from the headline and subhead alone, what would a stranger think this is, who it is for, and what to do next? Say where that breaks down.
2. Clarity and specificity: quote up to five weak lines (vague, jargon, feature-without-benefit) and rewrite each.
3. Proof: what claims lack evidence? What proof is missing for a visitor who is {{skepticism}} about this offer?
4. Objections: list the top three unanswered objections and where on the page to answer each.
5. Calls to action: assess wording, placement and friction. Suggest two alternative CTA labels.
6. Top five changes ranked by expected impact on {{goal}}, each with a one-line reason.

Rules: quote the original text when criticizing it. Do not invent testimonials, numbers or features; use [placeholder: what is needed] where proof is missing. Keep the voice of the original unless it is the problem.

Format: numbered sections matching the above, then a final "Revised hero section" with a headline, subhead and CTA.

prompts.exampleOutput:
## 1. First-five-seconds test
A stranger learns almost nothing. "Project management" fits hundreds of products, "modern teams" names nobody, and the button says "Submit", which promises no outcome. Visitors from a search for agency planning software will not see their term or their problem.

## 2. Weak lines, rewritten
- "The Future of Project Management" -> "Plan every agency project without overbooking your team"
- "Powerful, seamless, all-in-one" -> "See who is free, who is stretched, and which deadlines are at risk, in one view"
- "Boost productivity" -> "Catch overbooked weeks before they cost you a deadline"
- "Collaborate better" -> "Share one live schedule instead of chasing status in chat"

## 3. Proof
"Great tool!" has no name, role or result. Add [placeholder: named customer, role, agency size, and a measurable outcome]. A somewhat skeptical visitor also needs a screenshot of the real schedule view.

## 4. Unanswered objections
1. "Will my team actually use it?" -> add setup time and a short walkthrough under the hero.
2. "What does it cost?" -> show price near the CTA.
3. "Can I move my data?" -> note spreadsheet import.

Replace "Submit" with "Start my free trial" or "Plan my first project". Add "No card needed" beneath it.

1. Rewrite headline for the agency use case.
2. Change the button label.
3. Add a real product screenshot.
4. Replace the testimonial.
5. Surface pricing and no-card note.

**Plan every project without overbooking your team**

[Start my free trial] No card needed

prompts.title: Customer persona from reviews
prompts.description: Synthesize real customer reviews or survey answers into evidence-backed personas, jobs to be done and messaging language.
prompts.body:
You are a customer research analyst. Using only the text below, build up to {{persona_count}} customer persona(s) for {{product}}.

Source material ({{source_type}}):
"""
{{reviews}}
"""

Instructions
1. Read everything first and list the recurring themes with a rough count of how many entries mention each.
2. For each persona include: a short descriptive name (not a fake human biography), who they are as far as the text shows, the job they hire the product for, triggers that made them look for a solution, top frustrations, what they value, and objections or doubts.
3. Support every claim with a short direct quote from the source and mark anything you infer rather than read as [inference].
4. Extract a "words they use" list: exact phrases customers use to describe problems and benefits. These are for copy and keywords.
5. Note what the data cannot tell us and what to ask in follow-up interviews.

Rules: do not invent demographics, job titles, ages or statistics that are not in the text. If the sample is too small or too uniform to justify separate personas, say so and give one.

Format: Themes table, then one section per persona, then Words They Use, then Gaps and Next Questions.

## Themes
| Theme | Mentions |

| Easy setup | 2 of 6 |

## Persona 1: The Pain-Driven Home Worker
- Who: works from a home table or small desk (3 of 6 entries).
- Job: stop physical discomfort without buying a whole new desk.
- Trigger: back or wrist pain after long sessions. "my back stopped hurting after two weeks"

prompts.title: Keyword clustering by search intent
prompts.description: Group a raw keyword list into topical clusters with intent labels, a primary keyword per page and a suggested content type.
prompts.body:
You are an SEO analyst. Cluster the keyword list below into groups that should each be targeted by one page.

Website or business: {{site}}
Goal for the content: {{goal}}

Keywords (one per line, optionally with monthly volume after a comma):
{{keywords}}

Method
1. Group keywords that a single page could satisfy, based on meaning and likely search intent, not just shared words.
2. Label each cluster's dominant intent: informational, commercial investigation, transactional or navigational.
3. Pick one primary keyword per cluster (highest volume among close synonyms, unless intent says otherwise) and list the supporting keywords.
4. Suggest a page type and a working page title for each cluster.
5. Flag keywords that need their own page despite similar wording, and any that are off-topic or should be dropped.
6. Rank clusters by priority for {{goal}}, with a one-line reason. If volume is missing, say that ranking is judgement only.

Rules: do not claim difficulty scores, rankings or SERP details you cannot see. Mark intent as a judgement that should be checked against actual search results.

Format: a table with columns Cluster, Intent, Primary keyword, Supporting keywords, Page type, Priority. Then a short list of flags and next steps.

| V60 vs Chemex | Commercial | v60 vs chemex | chemex coffee maker | Comparison article | 2 |
| Pour over how-to | Informational | how to make pour over coffee | how to use a v60 | Step-by-step guide | 3 |

## Flags
- "how to use a v60" could be its own page if you want to rank for brand-specific brewing; here it is merged with the general how-to.
- "coffee grinder for pour over" has a different buying need; consider a short section now and a dedicated page later.
- Priority is judgement based on volume and closeness to equipment sales; no difficulty data was provided.

## Next steps
Check each cluster's live search results to confirm intent before committing to the page type.
prompts.notes: Grouping by intent rather than shared words avoids splitting one topic across pages or cramming two intents into one. For big lists, run it in batches of 200-300 keywords and then merge clusters.

## Diagnosis
- Framing ("remote work is new") is outdated; most readers now run hybrid teams.
- "Always use Zoom": tool-specific advice, and the recommended tool changed. VERIFY any product names.
- "70% of remote workers feel isolated": VERIFY. No source or date.
- Tip 3 ("keep video on") is a policy, not a tip, and is debated.
- Missing: hybrid meetings, async alternatives, AI note-takers and consent.

## Update plan
Keep: agenda in advance, end on time. Rewrite: tool advice and recording tip. Cut: blanket video rule. Add: hybrid meeting setup, when to replace a meeting with an async update, AI note-taker and recording consent.

## Refreshed article
# Remote and Hybrid Team Meetings: 5 Tips That Work
*Updated [month year] for hybrid teams.*

Most teams now mix office and remote days, which makes meetings harder: half the room talks while the other half squints at a screen. These tips keep meetings short, fair and worth attending.

1. **Send the agenda a day early**, with the decision you need from the group.
2. **Give remote attendees the first word**, so they are not an afterthought.
3. **Use whatever video tool your team already knows.** Pick one and stick with it. [CITE: current tool comparison, if kept]
4. **End on time.** If a topic runs long, schedule a follow-up or move it to an async update.
5. **Share notes, not just recordings.** AI note-takers can help, but tell attendees first and get consent. Short written notes beat a 60-minute replay.

Feeling cut off is a real risk for remote staff. [CITE: current survey on workplace isolation]

## Metadata
Title: Remote and Hybrid Team Meetings: 5 Tips That Work
Meta (146): Practical tips for running remote and hybrid meetings: agendas, fair turn-taking, async alternatives and notes that people actually read.

## Change log
Reframed intro for hybrid; replaced Zoom tip; cut video rule; rewrote recording tip; added consent and async guidance; removed unsourced 70% statistic.

## Pre-publish checklist
Confirm every VERIFY and CITE item; test links; check recording laws for your regions; keep the URL slug; align internal links.

prompts.title: Competitor messaging teardown
prompts.description: Compare how competitors position themselves from their own copy and find messaging gaps you can credibly own.
prompts.body:
You are a competitive messaging analyst. I will paste copy from competitor pages. Analyze only that text.

My product: {{product}}
My target customer: {{customer}}
What I can honestly claim (strengths I can prove): {{strengths}}

Competitor copy (label each competitor):
"""
{{competitor_copy}}
"""

Tasks
1. For each competitor summarize: the audience they speak to, their main promise, claimed differentiators, proof they offer, tone, and the call to action.
2. Create a comparison table across competitors of the claims they make, such as speed, ease, price, support, security, integrations. Mark claims many competitors share as "table stakes".
3. Identify messaging gaps: customer concerns that no competitor addresses well. Note the evidence for each (or the lack of it).
4. Recommend {{num_angles}} angles I could credibly own, grounded in my strengths. For each give the angle, a sample headline, the proof needed, and the risk of using it.
5. List words and phrases to avoid because every competitor already uses them.

Rules: do not assume anything about competitors beyond the pasted text; do not invent features or pricing. Say plainly where the sample is too small to conclude.

Format: sections 1-5 with tables where useful.

variables.label: Target customer

variables.label: Competitor copy

Competitor A: 'The all-in-one work management platform. Plan, track and deliver projects at scale.' Trusted by 50,000 teams.
Competitor B: 'Project management that just works. Simple. Powerful. Flexible.' Free plan available.
Competitor C: 'Resource planning for agencies. Know who is working on what.' Integrations with 40+ tools.

prompts.exampleOutput:
## 1. Summaries
- **A:** speaks to large teams; promise is breadth ("all-in-one"); proof is scale (50,000 teams); tone corporate; CTA unknown.
- **B:** speaks to anyone; promise is simplicity; proof: free plan; tone casual.
- **C:** speaks to agencies; promise is visibility into resourcing; proof: 40+ integrations.

## 2. Claims table
| Claim | A | B | C | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Easy or simple | - | yes | - | emerging |
| Powerful or flexible | yes | yes | - | table stakes |
| Scale or trust | yes | - | - | |
| Agency focus | - | - | yes | |
| Integrations | - | - | yes | |

## 3. Gaps
No competitor addresses setup time, capacity warnings before deadlines slip, or planning from real calendar data. C comes closest but only claims visibility.

## 4. Angles
1. **Early warning:** "Know about overbooking before the deadline does." Proof needed: a demo or example. Risk: C may respond.
2. **Real calendars:** "Plans that reflect leave and meetings." Proof: product demo.
3. **Fast setup:** "From spreadsheet to plan in 20 minutes." Risk: unverified for large teams.

## 5. Words to avoid
"Powerful", "simple", "all-in-one", "flexible".

prompts.title: A/B test hypotheses and prioritization
prompts.description: Turn a weak-performing page or email into well-formed test hypotheses, ranked by impact and effort, with clean success criteria.

prompts.exampleOutput:
## Diagnosis
1. The headline gives no reassurance or framing, and 55% leave early (evidence: bounce rate).
2. Key doubts (per user pricing, cancellation) are answered only in a footer FAQ (evidence: prospect questions).
3. Plans look similar, so choosing is hard (evidence: feedback). Confirm with heatmaps or plan-click data.

## Hypotheses
1. Because prospects ask about cancellation, adding "14-day trial, cancel anytime" under the headline will increase trial starts. Control: "Pricing". Variant: "Simple pricing. Try it free for 14 days, cancel anytime."
2. Because buyers ask whether pricing is per user, labeling "per user per month" in bold on each plan and adding a team-cost example will reduce hesitation.
3. Because plans look alike, highlighting who each plan is for will help.
4. Because "Get started" is vague, "Start free trial" will increase clicks.

| Test | Impact | Confidence | Effort | Rank |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 4 | 4 | 1 | 1 |
| 4 | 2 | 3 | 1 | 2 |
| 2 | 3 | 3 | 2 | 3 |
| 3 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 4 |

## Top test details
At 1,000 visitors per week and a 1.2% baseline, only a large lift would be detectable in a month; expect around 8-10 weeks for a modest change. Guardrail: trial-to-paid conversion. Do not change pricing or layout meanwhile. If that is too slow, combine tests 1 and 4 as a single "messaging" variant.
